story: On January 28, 1986, Space Shuttle Challenger launched on mission STS-51-L, carrying a crew of seven including schoolteacher Christa McAuliffe. Just 73 seconds into flight at an altitude of 46,000 feet, the vehicle broke apart. Contrary to popular belief, the shuttle did not actually explode. Record-low temperatures of 36 degrees Fahrenheit at launch had stiffened the rubber O-rings in the right Solid Rocket Booster, causing a joint to fail and leak hot gas. This flame burned through an attachment strut to the external fuel tank, causing structural failure. As the vehicle traveled at Mach 1.92, overwhelming aerodynamic forces ripped the orbiter apart. While the crew compartment survived the initial breakup, investigators found that several emergency air packs had been manually activated, and the exact cause of death remains inconclusive.
angle: The Space Shuttle Challenger didn't actually explode—it was violently ripped apart by raw aerodynamic forces after a failed O-ring caused a structural collapse.

claims.claim: The cause of the disaster was the failure of primary and secondary O-ring seals in a joint on the right Solid Rocket Booster.

disputed: Whether audio recordings of the crew panicking during the fall exist (sources clarify that no voice recording exists and it is a legend).
